notes.title: eVisa and entry basics
notes.traveler_summary: Vietnam uses an official eVisa system for many travelers. Entry rules, permitted stay, and port eligibility should be checked before booking because airline check-in and border officers rely on the exact document details.
practical_guidance: Apply only through official or trusted channels.
Match passport details exactly, including names and dates.
Keep proof of onward travel, accommodation, and funds accessible.
watchouts: Third-party visa websites can look official.
A wrong entry port, typo, or expired passport can cause check-in or arrival problems.
Visa-free exemptions and Phu Quoc-specific rules can differ from ordinary entry.
examples: A traveler flying into Da Nang should make sure the eVisa entry point matches Da Nang International Airport.
A hotel booking screenshot is useful when asked about accommodation.

notes.title: Cash, ATMs, and card reality
notes.traveler_summary: Vietnam is still heavily cash-friendly for street food, markets, small cafés, taxis, homestays, and rural areas. Cards work better at hotels, malls, airlines, and higher-end restaurants.
practical_guidance: Carry small VND notes daily.
Use bank ATMs in secure, well-lit locations.
Confirm card surcharges before paying.
watchouts: ATMs may have withdrawal limits and fees.
Small vendors may not have change for large notes.
Some QR wallets are local-account focused and not easy for short visitors.
examples: A bánh mì stall may only take cash; a hotel in District 1 may take cards easily.
A market seller may struggle with a 500,000 VND note for a small purchase.

notes.title: Common traveler friction and scams
notes.traveler_summary: Most trips are smooth, but tourists should watch for taxi overcharging, confusing prices, unofficial tour sellers, shoe-cleaning or photo approaches, and motorbike rental disputes.
practical_guidance: Use ride-hailing apps or reputable taxi brands.
Agree prices before accepting services.
Photograph rental bikes and helmets before leaving.
watchouts: Airport taxi approaches can be confusing after long flights.
Very cheap tours may add shopping stops or weak operators.
Passport-as-deposit requests should be treated carefully.
examples: A fixed app fare is easier than negotiating while jet-lagged.
For scooters, document scratches and fuel level before riding.
notes.source_label: U.S. Department of State: Vietnam travel information

notes.title: Police and official interactions
notes.traveler_summary: Keep interactions calm, polite, and document-led. Hotels usually register foreign guests, and travelers should be able to show passport, visa, and accommodation details when needed.
practical_guidance: Carry your passport or keep it quickly accessible according to your risk comfort and hotel context.
Ask your hotel or embassy for help in serious situations.
Stay calm if stopped while riding or during document checks.
watchouts: Driving without the correct license/permit can create trouble.
Do not argue aggressively with police or officials.
Language gaps can escalate confusion.
examples: If stopped on a scooter, use translation and show documents rather than debating roadside.
If a passport is held by a hotel or rental operator, know where it is and how to retrieve it.
notes.source_label: U.S. Department of State: Vietnam travel information

notes.title: Crossing roads
notes.traveler_summary: Vietnamese city traffic can feel chaotic, especially in Ho Chi Minh City and Hanoi. Cross slowly and predictably; motorbikes flow around steady movement more easily than sudden stops.
practical_guidance: Use crossings and traffic lights when available.
Move steadily, keep looking, and avoid sudden backward steps.
Follow locals at complex junctions until you learn the rhythm.
watchouts: Phones, luggage, and panic stops make crossings riskier.
Buses and cars cannot flow around pedestrians like motorbikes can.
Rain reduces visibility and braking.
examples: A steady walk across a motorbike stream is safer than sprinting halfway and freezing.
At large roundabouts, wait for locals or choose an alternate crossing.

notes.title: Scooter and motorbike culture
notes.traveler_summary: Motorbikes are central to Vietnam travel, but self-driving is one of the biggest practical risk areas for visitors because of licensing, insurance, road conditions, traffic habits, and rental disputes.
practical_guidance: Use licensed guided tours if inexperienced.
Check travel insurance wording before riding.
Wear a proper helmet and avoid night/rain mountain riding.
watchouts: Many policies exclude riding without a valid license.
Mountain loops can have trucks, landslides, fog, animals, and poor road surfaces.
Rental shops may ask for passport deposits or charge for existing damage.
examples: The Ha Giang loop is not the same risk profile as a short beach-town scooter ride.
A GrabBike is often safer for city hops than self-driving in unfamiliar traffic.
notes.source_label: U.K. Foreign Travel Advice: Vietnam safety and security

notes.title: SIM and eSIM advice
notes.traveler_summary: Mobile data is a daily-use essential in Vietnam for maps, translation, ride-hailing, messaging, and delivery. Airport SIMs are convenient; city shops may be cheaper; eSIMs are easiest before arrival.
practical_guidance: Set up data before relying on ride-hailing at the airport.
Keep your passport handy for local SIM registration if required.
Download offline maps and translation packs.
watchouts: Airport packages can be more expensive or vague on data limits.
Coverage varies in mountains, caves, islands, and boat areas.
Some local apps require Vietnamese phone verification.
examples: An eSIM plus Grab already installed makes late arrivals easier.
Sapa trekking and Ha Long boat routes may have patchy coverage.

notes.title: Weather changes by region
notes.traveler_summary: Vietnam's long geography means there is no single best month for the whole country. Northern mountains, central coast, southern cities, and islands can have different rain, heat, typhoon, and cool-season patterns.
practical_guidance: Plan by region rather than country-wide averages.
Check typhoon and flood risk for central Vietnam in storm season.
Pack layers for Sapa/Da Lat and sun/rain gear for the south.
watchouts: Hoi An, Hue, and Da Nang can flood during heavy central rains.
Northern winter can be cold and damp.
Island boat trips can be cancelled by rough seas.
examples: A great beach month in Phu Quoc may still be cool or misty in Sapa.
Central Vietnam can have beautiful dry spells and serious storm disruptions in different months.
notes.source_label: Vietnam National Authority of Tourism: weather and climate

notes.title: Nightlife awareness
notes.traveler_summary: Vietnam has lively nightlife in major cities and beach areas. Practical issues are usually overcharging, drink awareness, late-night transport, noise, theft, and scooter risk after alcohol.
practical_guidance: Use app rides late at night.
Check menu prices and bills before ordering rounds.
Keep valuables close in crowded bar streets.
watchouts: Do not ride after drinking.
Some venues add service charges or inflated tourist prices.
Beach party areas and backpacker streets need ordinary nightlife caution.
examples: Bui Vien in HCMC is different from a quiet cocktail bar in Thao Dien.
Late-night GrabCar is often worth the extra cost after drinking.
notes.source_label: U.S. Department of State: Vietnam travel information

notes.title: Local etiquette basics
notes.traveler_summary: Vietnam is generally forgiving with visitors, but modest dress at temples, calm bargaining, respect for elders, careful photography, and face-saving politeness go a long way.
practical_guidance: Dress modestly at religious and memorial sites.
Bargain with a smile and walk away politely if needed.
Ask before photographing people closely.
watchouts: Do not touch people's heads or use feet to point at people or sacred objects.
Public arguments can embarrass everyone and make resolution harder.
War, politics, and national symbols deserve care.
examples: A friendly market bargain is normal; insulting the seller is not.
At temples, covered shoulders and quiet movement are safer defaults.
